method: External web-search research on all 50 ideas (competitors, demand signals, price comparables), carried out by Hans's research assistant in November 2026 (top 10 first, the other 40 after). Sources are named as found; none of the figures or claims has been re-verified by this site. Verify before relying on any of it.
caveat: As researched November 2026 by web search; verify before relying on it. Verdicts are a reading of the evidence found, not a forecast.

tariff-lamp.summary: No standalone competing product was found (Tibber Pulse's light shows connection status, not price), while several independent DIY builds do exactly this, and dynamic tariffs are a real, growing NL/DE category (Tibber, EDF FreePhase, Nord Pool-indexed contracts).
tariff-lamp.risk: Technical users can DIY it with a cheap smart bulb and Home Assistant; the product has to beat "just buy a smart plug" on simplicity.

smiley-terminal.summary: HappyOrNot, the dominant incumbent, is confirmed subscription-only at roughly $69–100 per kiosk per month (Fox Business, Software Advice, Spendbase); four terminals at $69 a month is about $3,300 a year against a one-off buy, so payback is under two months. No competitor was found selling a comparable buy-once terminal (SurveyStance and AirVote are subscription or freemium).
smiley-terminal.risk: No public complaints about HappyOrNot's cost or lock-in surfaced (reviews are thin and positive), so the pain point is assumed, not verified; there is no direct evidence facility managers are shopping for a buy-once alternative.

club-scoreboard.summary: Full-size varsity boards run about $5,000–5,700 (Anthem Sports, School Health / Sportable); mid-tier portable wireless units about $2,089 (First Team FT810W); Daktronics is quote-only. Demand evidence: a Silicon Chip article calls pro boards generally out of reach for amateur and school teams, an Electro-Tech-Online thread shows a club rejecting pre-built units as too costly and asking how to DIY one, and a Make Magazine piece covers a parent building one for the same reason.
club-scoreboard.risk: All demand evidence is anecdotal; nobody has quantified what clubs will pay. Also: at €399 the board is roughly a fifth of the mid-tier and a twelfth of the full-size price, so the pitch's "a fifth of the price" should name which tier it compares to.

fire-door-watch.summary: The UK Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022, regulation 10, legally mandate quarterly fire-door checks in buildings over 11 m, an enforced compliance duty. The market is already populated: Safecility ShutSafe (NB-IoT, subscription), Minol Connect / B.One, Harmony Auro Door, Fireco DorMag Pro and Loxone all sell open-door or gap sensing with remote monitoring today. Harmony claims over a third of fire doors cannot be annually inspected because of access problems, so a gap remains.
fire-door-watch.risk: Not a novel niche: it needs a clear wedge (no-subscription LoRaWAN) against funded incumbents with existing housing-association relationships. Incumbent per-door pricing could not be confirmed (quote-based).

hallway-transit-board.summary: More than ten independent DIY e-paper transit displays were found across UK, DE, CH, US and Canada (busink, pibus, rpi_waiting_time_display, rmv-rpi-display, transit-pi, E-Ink Trainstation, a Swiss CFF display, Munich / BVG / BART / GO Transit plugins for TRMNL): repeated, geographically spread reinvention is a classic pre-product buy signal. No ready-made consumer product fills the gap; B2B stop-display vendors (Luminator, Papercast, ConnectPoint) sell to transit agencies. TRMNL, a general e-ink dashboard with community transit plugins, sells at $149.95–219, which supports the €119–149 band.
hallway-transit-board.risk: Every known instance is a DIY build, not a purchase; willingness to pay for a finished, no-soldering version is unproven.

meter-eye.summary: The DIY precedent is real and active: jomjol's AI-on-the-edge-device (ESP32-CAM + TFLite) has an actively maintained ESP32-S3 successor board covered by CNX Software and Electronics-Lab in 2025. Multi-year German-language threads on ioBroker and heimnetz.de show real users hitting setup friction (digit misreads, ROI and alignment tuning), exactly the gap a finished product fixes. No assembled commercial competitor was found at this price.
meter-eye.risk: Community size could not be confirmed numerically; one forum mentioned possible EU Data Act friction around camera-based meter reading, unverified and worth a legal check before launch.

sg-ready-price-switch.summary: SG-Ready is confirmed as a real certified German standard (BWP) supported by most EU heat-pump makers (NIBE, Viessmann, Vaillant). Installers and owners actively discuss wiring dynamic-tariff logic to SG-Ready with DIY tools (Shelly relay + Home Assistant, evcc, the Tibber app) on HaustechnikDialog and in the simon42 / evcc communities. Germany's BEG funding rules reportedly require a digital grid-control interface on new heat pumps from July 2027.
sg-ready-price-switch.risk: A cheap DIY substitute already exists (Shelly relay at roughly €30–40 plus free Home Assistant or evcc), and one forum voice called plain SG-Ready "not very useful" without extra conditions. The real market is installers wanting a no-fuss, no-cloud box to resell, which matches the pack's B2B kill question.

shop-window-epaper-signs.summary: Enterprise ESL vendors (Pricer, Hanshow) target chains with thousands of SKUs; independent-grocer sources (DUMAC, RetailWire) name upfront cost as the top objection because independents cannot spread it like chains. A Shopify Community thread confirms no plug-and-play, no-subscription ESL kit exists today. Bare e-paper hardware costs about $47–113; enterprise gateways (not needed here) add $300–400, which makes a €119 finished no-gateway unit plausible on margin.
shop-window-epaper-signs.risk: Nothing confirms an underserved category at scale, only that the big players do not serve it; independents may keep using a €2 chalk sign.

accessible-midi-instrument.summary: Direct competitors are active: Skoog (about £180–230), Cosmo / Filisia (about $199 per dot), AptiPlay (open source, pitched as the cheaper DIY alternative) and the older Device One / One6 from Drake Music Project NI. The OHMI Trust (UK, Arts Council-funded) exists because adapted instruments are not cheap, confirming a funding-constrained institutional buyer class looking for lower-cost options. €299 sits above Skoog and Cosmo but far below Soundbeam (£2,505–4,595 for a full kit).
accessible-midi-instrument.risk: Skoog and Cosmo already occupy this niche at lower prices; €299 has to clearly beat a $199 Skoog, not match it.

build-a-radio-kit.summary: Elenco's WEmake FM soldering kit sells at about £31–47, with volume pricing around $43 at 25+ units: a real category with real demand, already owned by an established, cheaper incumbent.
build-a-radio-kit.risk: Needs a clear differentiator (laser-cut case, no-code angle) to win a teacher's budget over Elenco.

fruiting-chamber-controller.summary: Real DIY precedent: ShroomBox (Blynk) and Raspberry Pi builds combine Inkbird CO2 and humidity controllers to hit the stated RH and CO2 targets, and a documented "fan and humidifier fighting each other" failure mode is exactly what a purpose-built controller fixes.
fruiting-chamber-controller.risk: Inkbird units cost under €50 each; the integrated unit must clearly beat "buy two Inkbirds and wire them yourself".

half-keyboard.summary: Maltron one-handed keyboards run about $540–970 and the Matias Half-Keyboard from about $654, which confirms and even understates the pitch's "€500 incumbents". A €149–199 entrant undercuts every named incumbent three to five times.
half-keyboard.risk: A price gap does not confirm clinical adoption by occupational therapists; that is what the ten-OT trial in the kill question is for.
rows: Maltron one-handed keyboard (MaxiAids, School Health, SpecialNeedsComputers.ca)

hay-spear.summary: Self-heating hay and straw fires are real and well documented, with defined danger thresholds (about 65–95 °C / 150–200 °F). Quanturi's HAYTECH already sells a bale-insertion probe and repeater system, so this is a direct incumbent, not greenfield.
hay-spear.risk: Incumbent pricing and MOQ, and the insurer channel's interest, are unverified.
rows: University of Kentucky / Oneida County hay-fire guides
The problem is real and documented

nfc-voice-labels.summary: PenFriend (RNIB-affiliated, about $180) is the dominant incumbent but is barcode-based, not NFC, which confirms the NFC plus washable-sticker approach as a real gap. A DIY app (VoiceTag) validates the concept's appeal.
nfc-voice-labels.risk: PenFriend is deeply entrenched with blind-support organisations; displacing institutional buying habits is the real challenge, not features.

sip-coaster.summary: A real, funded category: Aquarate / Hydracare is live in UK care homes, Person Centred Software sells weighing "smart cups", and Aquatime was EU-funded. The incumbents are smart cups that measure actual consumption, not coasters, so a more direct solution already exists; a Nottingham Trent student project built almost exactly this coaster.
sip-coaster.risk: Must win on cost and simplicity against institutionally adopted smart-cup competitors.

touchless-switch-module.summary: Several Chinese OEM/ODM makers advertise touchless-dispenser capability, mostly simple IR proximity rather than gesture recognition. No evidence was found of an established market for a standalone drop-in gesture module sold to EU OEMs, as opposed to sourcing complete cheap dispensers.
touchless-switch-module.risk: The module layer itself may not be a market, only a design choice inside someone else's product.
rows: OEMs buy finished dispensers, not modules

uvb-lamp-checker.summary: Solarmeter 6.5R, the established incumbent, sells at about $228–280 (up to about €488 in the EU), three to five times the €59–89 target: a genuine price gap. Lamp fade is the real stated problem and the reason this meter category exists.
uvb-lamp-checker.risk: Solarmeter is trusted in a safety-relevant niche (animal welfare); a cheaper entrant must earn accuracy trust, not just win on price.

haccp-fridge-logger.summary: A real, heavily served category (Testo Saveris 2 / Food, Checkit), but pricing and licensing sit behind sales quotes, so "no monthly fee" cannot be confirmed as a genuine gap rather than a restatement of what is already offered. FridgeTag, named in the pack, returned no results and may be discontinued.
haccp-fridge-logger.risk: The buy-once wedge is unverified against incumbents' actual terms; one hardware-only listing at CHF 445 was the only open price found.
rows: Named in the pack; no results found

modbus-pocket-analyser.summary: No handheld device marketed specifically as a Modbus/RS485 bus analyser for HVAC or solar technicians was found, only adjacent refrigerant and system tools (Fieldpiece, Mastercool). This could be genuine white space or a niche that general search does not index well (industrial and BMS channels).
modbus-pocket-analyser.risk: Absence of evidence is not a gap confirmed; check industrial-distribution catalogues and ask technicians before reading it as white space.

workshop-dust-sentinel.summary: The underlying hazards are well documented (NIOSH and CDC on 3D-printer VOCs in makerspaces), but no regulated indoor-air-quality standard for small workshops was found, which undercuts the "documentation for health-and-safety visits" framing.
workshop-dust-sentinel.risk: Demand may be real but voluntary, not compliance-forced.
rows: Same; no regulatory threshold for small workshops found

cell-grader.summary: Dedicated 18650/21700 testers already exist commercially (ZB206+, generic capacity and internal-resistance testers), confirming the technology is real and buildable, but no evidence was found of repair cafés or rebuild shops actively seeking grading tools.
cell-grader.risk: Demand is unverified rather than contradicted; the kill question's fifteen commitments are the test.

farm-shop-self-checkout.summary: Unstaffed farm retail is real and growing in Germany (about 600 smart stores, about 150 in farm retail) on existing systems (Dorfladenbox, Ackerpay), and case studies show farms moving from vending to self-checkout successfully. But a 2026 study cited in the research found self-checkout correlates with higher shrinkage, not lower, which directly undercuts the kill question's "less shrinkage than the honesty box" test.
farm-shop-self-checkout.risk: The kill metric may be wrong: uptime, basket size or customer satisfaction may be better go/no-go measures than shrinkage. Hans should decide.
rows: Farm moved from vending to self-checkout

correction.title: Kill-question metric questioned by research (November 2026)
correction.text: The kill question passes if five farm shops report less shrinkage than the honesty box. A 2026 study found in the research reports the opposite correlation for self-checkout in general: more shrinkage, not less. The category itself is real and growing (Dorfladenbox, Ackerpay, Locafox case studies), so the idea stands, but the pass mark may be measuring the wrong thing. Before running the pilot, decide with the shops what success means: uptime, basket size, customer satisfaction, staff hours saved. Kill question unchanged pending Hans's decision. As researched November 2026 by web search; verify before relying on it.

frost-sentinel.summary: The frost-warning category is real and established (Pessl / METOS frost products, Sencrop, a UK-funded Terraprima / Vinewatch project), confirming funded institutional interest, but no competitor pricing was found anywhere (quote-only is the norm), so the "no €1,400 weather station" comparison is unverified either way.
frost-sentinel.risk: The price claim in the pitch is unsupported until a competitor quote is in hand.
rows: METOS viticulture brochure; METOS frost leaflet (Pessl)
IoT World Today: smart vineyard frost device

school-scope.summary: Classroom pocket-oscilloscope kits exist (Velleman / Whadda WSEDU06 at about £19–38, ConsuLab uScope classroom sets), confirming a real buyer and category; the cheap options get mixed-to-poor reviews, while deeper alternatives (PicoScope) are bench instruments, not pocket kits, so a quality gap in the middle is plausible.
school-scope.risk: Needs to justify a two-to-three-times price premium over Whadda on quality and curriculum grounds.

sound-to-light-alert.summary: Sonic Alert is a real, established incumbent selling individual components at about $64–224 each (one bundle discontinued) rather than one cheap integrated kit. "A third of today's prices" is roughly plausible: a full Sonic Alert setup is $150–250+ in parts against one €129–179 kit.
sound-to-light-alert.risk: A discontinued Sonic Alert all-in-one starter kit suggests this exact sub-segment may have been tried and pulled before; find out why.
rows: The integrated-kit segment was tried before

switchboard-hotspot-watch.summary: Panel hot-spot monitoring is real and actively developed (Eaton, GraceSense HSM 600, NFPA 70B cited as a compliance driver, a FAU / Siemens thermopile thesis), but everything found is enterprise-scale with no per-unit pricing, so €299–399 cannot be benchmarked.
switchboard-hotspot-watch.risk: The need may be served today mainly by periodic professional IR-camera inspection; vendors position sensors as a complement to inspection, not a replacement.

footfall-counter.summary: Camera-free, privacy-safe people counting is an established category (Terabee thermal / time-of-flight, FootfallCam hashing, Ariadne consent-free analytics), and the compliance angle is real and current, with the EU AI Act as a tailwind. No public pricing was found, so "a third of the incumbents' price" is unverifiable.
footfall-counter.risk: The price claim is unsupported; the differentiation must be proven on compliance and simplicity.

haptic-setpoint-knob.summary: The concept is validated by patents and one shipping product, the Aqara Touchscreen Dial V1, which is locked to Aqara's ecosystem; no cross-platform "works with any hub" haptic dial was found, matching the pitch's gap.
haptic-setpoint-knob.risk: Aqara, well funded, could extend its dial to more hubs faster than a newcomer establishes the category.
rows: Shipping haptic dial, Aqara ecosystem only
Prior art to check before launch

new-flat-air-check.summary: Direct-reading formaldehyde and VOC meter rentals exist (Extech VFM200, PCE meters) but are aimed at professionals, not consumer-facing retailer loan units; no furniture or flooring retailer loan-at-the-till programme was found, matching the pitch's channel angle. A pricier lab-analysed service (Wellbuild Lab, $395–525 a week) confirms willingness to pay at a much higher price point.
new-flat-air-check.risk: No evidence yet that retailers want to run a loan-unit programme; that channel is the actual kill question and is unverified.
rows: Willingness to pay at a higher price

quiet-guardian.summary: Passive, camera-free elderly-monitoring kits for family use are a real, populated category: IvedaCare ($500 + $50 a month), StillWell ($349 + about $49 a month), Blissfull Sense (about €460) and Caregiver Smart Solutions ($147–294 + $4–12 a month) all ship today, all with a subscription. The pack's "€2,500 lamp" reference could not be verified.
quiet-guardian.risk: Every real competitor charges an ongoing subscription; the near-subscription-free pitch is the differentiator and is unproven against entrenched competitors.

trinkwasser-logger.summary: The research could not confirm that continuous temperature logging itself (as opposed to periodic Legionella laboratory testing) is a legal requirement; in the pack that is an assumption, not a cited rule. Techem and Minol already own the property-manager relationship through their testing services.
trinkwasser-logger.risk: Soften the compliance-mandate language until checked against the TrinkwV §31 text directly, and consider selling through Techem or Minol as a channel rather than direct to property managers.

offline-ai-docent.summary: No fully offline museum kiosk product was found; every real deployment (Intuiface, the Autun Museum chatbot, a Warsaw exhibition chatbot, TimeLens at the Grand Egyptian Museum) depends on a network or cloud call, which supports "fully offline, no cloud" as a genuine technical differentiator.
offline-ai-docent.risk: No evidence museums actually want offline over cloud; the gap found is architectural, not a stated customer complaint.

pollinator-counter.summary: Insect Detect (peer-reviewed in PLOS ONE, open source, deployed across Europe through the SEPPI project) is a direct precedent validating the technical approach and a research-buyer channel; researchers report it is more time-efficient than manual transect counts. An Oregon State bumblebee camera-trap study corroborates.
pollinator-counter.risk: All known instances are research prototypes, not commercial products; this would be the first to commercialise a proven approach, not an entry into a validated commercial market.
